items.title: “a little scary”: Warframe’s studio opens Soulframe’s free PC alpha to everyone
items.summary: Soulframe, the fantasy action RPG from Warframe developer Digital Extremes, has opened its free early alpha to Windows PC players. The Open Preludes test
items.content:
This article needs JavaScript to display. Please turn on JavaScript in your browser and reload the page. Soulframe, the fantasy action RPG from Warframe developer Digital Extremes, has opened its free early alpha to Windows PC players. The Open Preludes test began November 6, removing the need to wait for an invitation to try the in-development game.

Players can create an account and download the standalone client from the official Soulframe website . The Steam page currently offers a wishlist, not the alpha download. This is an early test rather than Soulframe’s finished release.

Creative director Geoff Crookes described the decision as “a little scary” in a Digital Extremes announcement, saying the larger group of players can give the team feedback as development continues.

Soulframe puts players in the role of an Envoy fighting a corruption spreading through the world of Alca. Digital Extremes describes combat using weapons and abilities granted through Pacts with Omen Beasts, alongside story quests called Fables.

Exploration, releasing captive creatures and completing Fables open up additional systems, including crafting and social features. The studio says players can form parties of up to four to explore or take on challenges together.

The test is free, although optional Founder packs are offered separately. Players should expect unfinished systems, updates and possible bugs; access to the alpha should not be confused with a final launch date or a Steam release.

Digital Extremes says a separate update called Verse of the Veilands is due in November. It plans to add a world progression system and Omen Wolf mounts, alongside new features including fishing additions. The announcement does not give an exact day for that update.

To raise a wolf into a mount, players will need to train a pup, purify two Veilands regions and prepare a Bairnday Biscuit, according to the studio. The developer says the feature will continue to develop in later updates.

The update is also expected to bring a new Ode Shrike Pact with traps and other tools. Those additions are planned content; check the current patch notes for what has actually arrived before setting out to unlock them.

items.title: 5 Best Video Games Like Helldivers
items.summary: Depending on what you like about the "Helldivers" video game franchise, we have a little list of other game recommendations that you should check out.
items.content:
Arrowhead Game Studios Add SVG on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover "Helldivers" offers some of the most intense, rewarding, and cooperative gameplay that you'll find anywhere. While it's a completely PvE experience, you still feel like you're playing a multiplayer game thanks to the plot, which tasks you and every other player with fending off an alien invasion of Super Earth. Due to this unique plot and blend of genres, it can be difficult to find another game similar to "Helldivers," but there are certainly some out that are worth your time.

When it comes to searching for these other games, though, you'll have to know exactly what it is that keeps driving you to play "Helldivers," and that includes both the original and sequel. Whether it's the co-op gameplay, the intense PvE loop, or the constant progression in "Helldivers," several games offer rewarding playthroughs with these elements at the forefront. There are five games that stand out from the rest of the crowd, however, and you can see which games are most similar to "Helldivers" in the list below.

Fatshark "Warhammer 40,000: Darktide" might have the closest experience to the moment-to-moment gameplay in "Helldivers." It's a co-op, PvE game where you have an overarching goal always present during the story. However, the gameplay features individual missions that you and your teammates can complete to earn additional upgrades for your character. These missions consist of different maps, enemies, and objectives, and none of them are easy to get through.

Of course, you have your teammates by your side if you get into trouble, and you'll need them to survive certain parts of the maps, as venturing off solo can have dire consequences. As you progress in "Warhammer 40,000: Darktide," though, you'll continue to upgrade your character through unique traits and skills that are unlocked as part of your specific class.

The combat in "Warhammer 40,000: Darktide" is much grittier and closer-range than it is in "Helldivers," but the basics are easy enough to get the hang of until you start learning more in-depth strategies. If you're looking for a co-op game that's structured essentially the same as "Helldivers," "Warhammer 40,000: Darktide" is arguably the best choice.

Coffee Stain Publishing Visually, you'll notice some major differences between "Deep Rock Galactic" and "Helldivers." "Deep Rock Galactic" is more of an animated game set in Dwarven mines, with vibrantly colored maps and textures. If you take a deeper look at the game, though, the similarities with "Helldivers" begin to appear. "Deep Rock Galactic" can be played solo or in a party of up to four players, and the best experience sees you playing with at least one friend.

In any case, the game features procedurally generated levels where your goal is to exterminate an alien force by any means necessary. However, the aliens are a lot stronger than they seem, and your initial weapons that you start with usually won't be enough to get the job done. Luckily, "Deep Rock Galactic" lets you mine, forage, and gather resources on the fly during a mission so you can craft your own weapons and gear.

Using everything at your disposal, you'll gun down the alien enemies in a fast-paced, first-person environment where each level presents unique challenges and opportunities for survival. If you can past the cartoonish graphics, "Deep Rock Galactic" is one of the best gaming experiences in the modern era , especially in co-op.

Digital Extremes "Warframe," one of the best free-to-play games of all-time , is a futuristic MMO looter shooter that can be played solo, but the game emphasizes co-op as the premier way to play. The gameplay in "Warframe" flows much differently than it does in "Helldivers," as you have access to several open world areas as well as a social hub where you can interact with other real players. However, the game still offers unique missions where you have a set objective against PvE enemies that you can take on by yourself or with friends/strangers.

At the start of "Warframe," you'll design a character, also called a Tenno, and pick a certain class that determines your skills and overall playstyle. You can upgrade your character throughout the course of the game, which progresses as you complete story missions and take part in free-to-play expansions that arrive via content updates.

"Warframe" offers frantic and fast-paced third-person gameplay featuring a large number of enemies and some tough-to-beat bosses. You'll certainly find some similarities to "Helldivers" when playing "Warframe," but it's more of a live-service game that you won't ever truly finish.

2K If the co-op aspect of "Helldivers" is what you enjoy most about the game, then why not play one of the best co-op games of all-time ? "Borderlands 2," released way back in 2012, has remained one of the most celebrated open-world games, even a decade after its launch. While it's a solo game by default, you can complete an entire playthrough in a co-op party of four players or two players in local splitscreen co-op.

The theme, gameplay, and graphics in "Borderlands 2" don't offer many similarities to "Helldivers." "Borderlands" as a franchise has become iconic for its humorous dialogue, quirky characters, and unique animated graphics. While that might put off a "Helldivers" player who enjoys the dark and military-based gameplay of the series, all "Borderlands 2" needs is a shot to capture your interest. The story is immediately gripping, the class-based characters make combat unique, and the open-world exploration makes your time in the game fly by. Not to mention, you'll receive more weapons, gear, and equipment than you'll know what to do with.

Embark Studios "Arc Raiders" is in a unique spot if you're looking for a game similar to "Helldivers." On one hand, "Arc Raiders" is a co-op third-person extraction shooter with gun-based combat and PvE elements. However, on the other hand, "Arc Raiders" also features PvP combat, meaning you can run into other real players who can kill you, take your loot, and leave you without any exfil options.

items.title: Warframe: Tau Coming In December
items.summary: Your remarkable journey is about to lead to an era-defining trip to the Tau System, where new worlds ripe for exploration are waiting. Jump back into Warframe today and get ready to experience our most expansive update ever this December. 6
items.content:
Your remarkable journey is about to lead to an era-defining trip to the Tau System, where new worlds ripe for exploration are waiting. Jump back into Warframe today and get ready to experience our most expansive update ever this December.

67TH WARFRAME: BRYSKO

Hit the streets of Fornax as Brysko, the world-weary, noir-inspired detective brought to life with an inner monologue voiced by Matt Mercer. Enforce your own brand of street justice with an indomitable suite of Abilities, trusty Hound Companion and signature armaments like the Rain & Shine Fist Weapons and Corecracker Exalted Pistol. Brysko also introduces the first in a new class of premium Customizations: the Chimera Skin. As with a Protoframe, you'll be able to switch between his Warframe and Chimera aspects on the fly for a more Sentient appearance and voice-acted dialogue.

TAU STAR CHART

Your evolution continues in a new region of space beyond anything you've ever known: the Tau System. While there will remain much to do in the Origin System going forward, you'll also be able to enter Missions and explore new worlds across Tau. December will start you off with the mob-run ring city of Fornax, as well as the badlands of Perita, with many more planned for future updates.

PERITA

Although Perita thrived following the events of The Old Peace, its ecosystem has since collapsed into a hostile desert populated by feuding clans of Dazannah — and where both resources and allies are notoriously difficult to come by. With the last unconquered clan facing existential peril, its chieftain’s young son, Catulast, seeks help from its ancient foe, the Tenno. Will you brave the wasteland and answer its call?

items.title: I Underestimated The New Icebind Game Mode in Warframe – Opinion
items.summary: The new Icebind game mode in Warframe is an excellent new idea that finally launched after being delayed, here is a critique of it.
items.content:
A couple of days ago, I wrote an article venting my frustrations and disappointment in the recent update in Warframe , the Iceblade of Narin. Having the grind for her and her weapons locked to already existing game modes with their own loot pools, bloating the drop chances, felt like a miss to me. All the while, the way it was the send-off update before we ramp up for Tau felt a little underwhelming overall. In a recent update, Digital Extremes added the endgame game mode that was delayed, the “Icebind,” and it fixes one problem I had listed in that previous article, and another longstanding issue with Digital Extremes’ approach to endgame content, while also adding a few issues of its own.

The Icebind is the newest game mode in Warframe that was originally delayed from the Iceblade of Narin update . It is a 6-player, endgame-focused activity that requires manually inviting people to do it. The Icebind has 4 different game modes you can choose from, including:

How this game mode differs is set modifiers and very harsh conditions, including enemies at level 999 and above. As well as only allows one player to use a specific warframe in the squad. This means that you cannot stack 5 Dantes and a Harrow to avoid every harsh condition. This game mode also opts for additional side objectives that, if you start and fail, you fail the mission overall. Completing the side objectives gives you extra keys to acquire loot at the end of the mission.

With all of this out in the open, how does this game mode actually land? Well, I think it lands very well on its own two feet and feels much more rewarding and enjoyable as opposed to the weekly Archimedea runs that have become feeling a little outdated. It is a refresh of the endgame approach for Warframe and one that is definitely welcome, so long as there are aims to improve it.

The Icebind puts 6 players into already existing game modes with side objectives, when I feel the new objectives could have been their own game modes altogether. The side objectives are an interesting mix of new ideas. For example, players have to stand in a line to link up power from one place to another. A giant ice shrine you need to do a lot of DPS to break the bubbles around it. Not to mention a bubble that marks areas around it that are safe and unsafe to jump around to avoid getting hit. And a chest that requires keys dropped by enemies to open by standing next to said chest.

They do not sound really interesting on their own, but they are fun in practice so long as players understand what they are doing. My biggest concern about the integration here is how these new objectives are just optional challenges in already existing game modes when they feel like they could have been mixed into one game mode that goes from one step to the next. For example, the power chain being the opening objective, then the orb with the little “Simon says” area around it following the chain, then leading into that DPS check with the ice shrine before needing to do the chest as the final objective to unlock extraction.

Obviously, I know making these objectives optional in the existing game modes made it easier for players to engage in. But if there are going to be more experimentation for endgame content with this type of stuff, a dedication to the new ideas as opposed to old ones would be a better way to go, to me at least. This game mode does correct one issue in the overall update, however. That being how Narin is integrated into the wider narrative.

In my previous article critiquing the general update, I mentioned how there was a complete absence of narrative integration for Narin. I was not aware that the integration would be worked into the Icebind, instead of a dedicated mission for when you are farming for Narin. It’s a subversion that I wasn’t expecting, but I do understand what Digital Extremes were going for now. The only little bit of inconsistency is the lack of the murmur.

Seeing as the Icebind makes references to the Hex and the Indifference worming its way further into the origin system. I feel the murmur should have been the only enemy for narrative cohesion. As it stands, however, it is better worked in now, and I feel better about the update overall. I do look forward to hearing more explanations as the weeks progress with the Icebind.

Finally, the rewards are weirdly misrepresented. When the rewards were shown off originally, I assumed stuff like the Kuva were going to be bad-luck RNG drops. As some of us know from sorties/archon hunts. Luckily, that is not the case. Every chest drops a random good item, like boosters, rivens, forma, etc on top of the Kuva. My only complaint about this system is having a singular forma in the same drop table as a forma bundle. Not to mention the Kuva amount from either drop feels low. I think adding some entropic Kuva to the drop tables would incentivise players more to get the cosmetics and other goodies from Melica.

Finally, the new Riven Splicers are great. I have zero complaints about how they function. I also appreciate that they are a guaranteed reward on top of everything earned in an Icebind run. This feature is an excellent overhaul to the Riven system for endgame players. Heck, my negative crit Phenmor riven has weak spot damage now. Which is a fantastically nasty combo with my Harrow.

With all of this out in the open. I would like to recommend that Digital Extremes keep going with this idea. I feel the Icebind is strangely more approachable than Archimedea right now. This is mostly due to the fact that they do not force you to play with frames and weapons you do not like or have proper builds for. Enticing players to use their best-of-the-best builds and weapons for singular mission runs is a great idea. I just feel like the objectives could be their own things. As well as touching up the reward pool for better consistency. As it stands, just asking for an Icebind group in recruitment chat or in Yuvan Peak works perfectly.

As the seasons change, so does the Origin System. And this October is no exception, with plenty of seasonal, returning, and brand new additions to occupy you as we draw ever closer to Warframe: Tau later this year. Watch for the following events this month:

EPOCH OPERATION: TAUBOUND

October 15 - November 17 A unique event unlike anything you've experienced to date, Epoch Operation: Taubound offers all eligible Tenno the chance to become a part of Warframe history. If you want to help open up a path to the Tau System, be sure to have your account ready by completing the "Vor's Prize" Quest before October 15. Players looking to pilot their Vessel for the first time can also complete The Hex and The Old Peace in order to access a new, permanent Prologue Quest setting up the Road to Tau. For full event details – including prerequisites and more – click here.

NIGHTS OF NABERUS

October 1 @ 11 a.m. ET - November 2 @ 11 a.m. ET Spooky season returns to the Origin System during our annual Halloween-inspired event, with Daughter releasing her inventory of new and returning seasonal Customizations in exchange for Mother Tokens. While Baro Ki'Teer will mark the occasion in the same unsettling fashion as last year (IYKYK), we're also mixing it up by bringing back the Hallowed Nightmares Tactical Alert, allowing you to face off against the fearsome Jack O'Naut for even more Naberus treats. For all the harrowing details, check out our Halloween 2026 Events post.

NEW GAME MODE: THE ICEBIND

October 7 Originally intended to ship alongside Iceblade of Narin as "Glacial Defiance," our new 6-player game mode was ultimately delayed to allow for additional development time and renamed to The Icebind. Accessible in-game starting October 7, these challenging, high-level Missions can be played up to three times weekly, allowing you to put your teamwork (and Loadouts) to the test for valuable Rewards. Visit the official Warframe Forums to learn more about the delay, and further details of the game mode itself.

PRINCESS MARGARET CANCER FOUNDATION QUEST

October 1 - October 31 PMCF Quest (formerly Quest to Conquer Cancer) returns for another October full of special Community streams, donation incentives and Conquera Customizations. Join us all month long and help support The Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation light the way towards a world free from the fear of cancer. Visit the Warframe PMCF Quest webpage for more information or donate directly here.

items.title: Warframe: Banshee Prime Build and Post Rework Review
items.summary: Banshee's little rework in the most recent update in Warframe is very nice and makes her pretty viable in all forms of content in game.
items.content:
In the most recent update for Warframe, the Iceblade of Narin , one of the oldest warframes in the game, got a slight touch-up to her abilities. This streamlined her for more accessibility to what she can bring to the table. Banshee has always been in a weird spot, as players who know how to use her can make her dangerous, but most players (me included) didn’t understand her properly; this one touch-up made her easier to understand and, as such, gave her a new lease on life. So much so that I finally picked her back up and figured her out. Below will be our site’s recommended build for her in 2026.

Below is the build for her, which uses no forma, as I am using her Prime variant. If you are using the normal Banshee you got for free, simply copy what you see below with the forma you need to spend:

To get one thing out of the way quickly, I subsumed her 4th ability for Cyte-09’s Evade ability. This gives her invisibility to synergize with her other abilities so long as you keep getting headshot kills. From here, it’s pretty standard, just mostly build for a balance of each stack, with most of it going to range. Just make sure to add Arcane Crepuscular from the Hex’s shop in 1999.

Below are the Archon Shards I landed on for her. These are purely for flavor, and you can swap them out for whatever you wish.

As stated previously, the touch-up to her abilities is quite nice. You aren’t rooted in place, and everything feels much easier to understand with her abilities. I do respect the decision they made not to completely rework her kit. Especially if we look at past reworks like Oberon’s. But this little touch-up made me enjoy using her more. I would highly recommend using the Dual Torxica with this build. This is due to the fact that those pistols give lingering cold procs to random enemies, slowing them down so you can hit the weak points created with Sonar. It’s a killer build for Steel Path and beyond in Warframe.

items.title: What if Stop Killing Games win? Anthem, SpaceCraft and Warframe devs on the "massive undertaking" of preserving an always-online game
items.summary: Game developers discuss the challenge of adapting an always-online game to run without official server support.
items.content:
Digging into the practicalities of production timeframes and local servers

Image credit: Digital Extremes Feature by Edwin Evans-Thirlwell News Editor Published on Aug. 1, 2026, 1:04 p.m. 80 comments Follow Anthem Sci-fantasy shooter Warframe is the sexy cyborg fruit of 13 years of updates and expansions, encompassing scores upon scores of quests, areas, plotlines, systems and characters, together with a huge quantity of player-made art. Much of Warframe's original design still exists within the game, however tweaked and refreshed: the developers have removed a few larger chunks, including the underloved PvP raids, but they've mostly sought to polish up aspects that have lost their lustre, while playing out stories that range from spacey self-referentiality to commentary on indentured work. Currently, the studio are reworking Banshee, a sonic avenger who formed part of the Warframe launch roster way back in 2013.

"I know the Warframe team has been talking about bringing back raids, and doing stuff with that," the game's original design director Scott McGregor told me, at this year's Tennocon expo. "But overall, there's a lot of stuff from Warframe that's been in there for a long, long time. For better or for worse. I think, as a team, instead of mostly turning it off, we either improve it, or we replace it with something better."

Given that commitment to retaining all the love and labour soaked into Warframe's foundations, I find it strange that Digital Extremes do not, according to McGregor, have any particular plans for ensuring that Warframe will survive, should Digital Extremes become unable to officially support it. While Warframe is a PvE-led experience, mostly played solo, there's no offline mode and no local server support. "I can't say that we've really thought that far in advance," McGregor told me, when I asked how Warframe might outlive Digital Extremes. "We just keep working on the game." In the event that the devs are forced to pull the plug, he quipped, Digital Extremes will "do the Canadian thing, and it will be the right thing."

It seems increasingly vital that the creators of online-required games like Warframe make plans for their afterlives. The 'live service' space that attracted so much investment in the 2010s now appears fatally saturated, with a few evergreen juggernauts straining for growth, while the likes of Concord and Highguard crumble to atoms within weeks or months of release. Some of these live service decommissionings have sparked a lasting outcry. When Ubisoft shuttered always-online racer The Crew , it inspired the formation of Stop Killing Games , a "consumer rights" crusade to stop publishers arbitrarily switching off access, and make the addition of offline modes, local server support, and similar 'end of life' functionality a legal requirement. SKG's broad argument isn't that publishers should have to fund online games in perpetuity, but that there should be an obligation to hand the game over to players somehow when the publisher decides, for whatever reason, to end support.

SKG have proposed or endorsed a variety of legislation across California, the European Commission, and the UK parliament. They've not had huge success winning over the politicians, with industry lobbyists like the Electronic Software Association pushing back, but they've certainly kept the subject of preservation in the headlines. Recently, Sony fuelled the fire by announcing plans to stop selling PlayStation games on discs , putting more power in the hands of digital publishers who may cut off your access to their catalogues at whim. Amid these larger changes, there have been a few more positive stories about individual cases of videogame preservation. Earlier this year, Might & Delight added an offline mode to their wonderful RPG strollalong Book of Travels . Thick as Thieves developers Otherside are currently working (amid layoffs) on peer-to-peer multiplayer for their Looking Glass-inspired burglary sim, so that player gangs can keep on robbing mansions after the servers evaporate.

Myself, I support SKG's overall goal of ensuring that storied online games don't vanish forever. I find it a little terrifying that a universe as florid and fizzy as Warframe doesn't have any legacy provisions in place, though I guess it's possible that McGregor – who is now design director for the up-and-coming Soulframe - is simply keeping the plans under his hat, to avoid fomenting the idea that Warframe is on its way out.

Still, I have reservations. I think SKG's organisers are selective in their case for videogame preservation. They've had relatively little to say about the biggest extinction event of the past couple years, the sudden deindexing of thousands of adult games on Steam and Itch at the behest of payment networks. You could justify this as the group having a focus and picking their battles. You could also comment that a self-described "gamer coalition" is more comfortable going to bat for a shiny triple-A racer than a queer visual novel with some "problematic" elements (an inhibition I admittedly struggle with myself, as a cisgender news writer).

I also think SKG's organisers need to put aside their flattening emotive rhetoric - which often makes signing a petition against an online RPG's retirement sound like storming the Bastille - and do a better job of expressing the practicalities of adding 'end of life' functionality. The difficulty of this varies hugely by the project, to the point that comparisons start to feel meaningless, but much depends on whether developers plan for it from the beginning.

Among this year's individual cases of games introducing offline modes is SpaceCraft, Shiro's starfaring mining and trading empire sim. "When we started developing SpaceCraft, quite early on we thought about players still being able to play offline in the far future in case servers are no longer available, so we created the game with that in mind," the company's CEO Nicolas Cannasse told me over email. "It was important for us as we wanted SpaceCraft to be both playable with many players collaborating together or by solo players that wanted only to trade with others but have their own progress."

Shiro did, admittedly, have to introduce the mode ahead of schedule, after a number of solo asteroid magnates complained about being forced to go online during SpaceCraft's early access launch. "It required significant effort, for example adding saves management and autosaves," Cannasse went on, "but our infrastructure was flexible enough to allow for that." The developers themselves have benefited from the offline mode, he said; they are able "to run any version of the game locally on their own machines, simplifying testing, debugging and day-day development."

Inevitably, adding such features to games that were never planned to exist outside official servers may be an absolute nightmare. In a video last year, former Dragon Age series producer Mark Darrah sketched out a grand plan for reviving Anthem , BioWare's defunct always-online RPG, as a singleplayer experience running on local servers. In the same video, he also revealed that Anthem did support local servers at one point before launch. After writing up Darrah's video, I contacted him over email to ask for more general thoughts about how games with mandatory online can be rescued from the scrapyard. The picture he painted was considerably less rosy.

While letting players run games on their own servers might seem straightforward – surely, it's just a question of popping the server code and documentation on Github? – Darrah observed that properly reworking games like this can be "a massive undertaking", with costs potentially running into the millions. The dedicated servers offered by publishers are generally optimised towards the maximum possible headcount, and the server code may not scale well in the hands of players and modders, though this is less of a problem for a co-op squad game like Anthem than an actual MMO, such as Eve Online. Running the server on your own PC in order to launch a hitherto always-online single player game might also screw things up, Darrah added, because again, the code might not be optimised for this: "the GPU may be exploited for odd things, for example."

Another problem is security. Darrah pointed out that any publisher retrospectively adding local server features would need to carry out an audit to ensure players aren't at risk of data breaches. "For a game like Anthem that shares code with other games, you would also want to ensure you aren't introducing a security issue for your other games," he continued. Anthem uses the same Frostbite tech as EA's blockbuster cardgame FC Ultimate Team, for example. As such, Darrah explained, adding local server support for Anthem might inadvertently give a hacker access to FC UT's backend.
